# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/regex-automata/0.4.14/src/regex_automata/lib.rs.html

# regex_automata/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)/*!
[2](https://docs.rs#2)This crate exposes a variety of regex engines used by the `regex` crate.
[3](https://docs.rs#3)It provides a vast, sprawling and "expert" level API to each regex engine.
[4](https://docs.rs#4)The regex engines provided by this crate focus heavily on finite automata
[5](https://docs.rs#5)implementations and specifically guarantee worst case `O(m * n)` time
[6](https://docs.rs#6)complexity for all searches. (Where `m ~ len(regex)` and `n ~ len(haystack)`.)
[7](https://docs.rs#7)
[8](https://docs.rs#8)The primary goal of this crate is to serve as an implementation detail for the
[9](https://docs.rs#9)`regex` crate. A secondary goal is to make its internals available for use by
[10](https://docs.rs#10)others.
[11](https://docs.rs#11)
[12](https://docs.rs#12)# Table of contents
[13](https://docs.rs#13)
[14](https://docs.rs#14)* [Should I be using this crate?](#should-i-be-using-this-crate) gives some
[15](https://docs.rs#15)reasons for and against using this crate.
[16](https://docs.rs#16)* [Examples](#examples) provides a small selection of things you can do with
[17](https://docs.rs#17)this crate.
[18](https://docs.rs#18)* [Available regex engines](#available-regex-engines) provides a hyperlinked
[19](https://docs.rs#19)list of all regex engines in this crate.
[20](https://docs.rs#20)* [API themes](#api-themes) discusses common elements used throughout this
[21](https://docs.rs#21)crate.
[22](https://docs.rs#22)* [Crate features](#crate-features) documents the extensive list of Cargo
[23](https://docs.rs#23)features available.
[24](https://docs.rs#24)
[25](https://docs.rs#25)# Should I be using this crate?
[26](https://docs.rs#26)
[27](https://docs.rs#27)If you find yourself here because you just want to use regexes, then you should
[28](https://docs.rs#28)first check out whether the [`regex` crate](https://docs.rs/regex) meets
[29](https://docs.rs#29)your needs. It provides a streamlined and difficult-to-misuse API for regex
[30](https://docs.rs#30)searching.
[31](https://docs.rs#31)
[32](https://docs.rs#32)If you're here because there is something specific you want to do that can't
[33](https://docs.rs#33)be easily done with `regex` crate, then you are perhaps in the right place.
[34](https://docs.rs#34)It's most likely that the first stop you'll want to make is to explore the
[35](https://docs.rs#35)[`meta` regex APIs](meta). Namely, the `regex` crate is just a light wrapper
[36](https://docs.rs#36)over a [`meta::Regex`], so its API will probably be the easiest to transition
[37](https://docs.rs#37)to. In contrast to the `regex` crate, the `meta::Regex` API supports more
[38](https://docs.rs#38)search parameters and does multi-pattern searches. However, it isn't quite as
[39](https://docs.rs#39)ergonomic.
[40](https://docs.rs#40)
[41](https://docs.rs#41)Otherwise, the following is an inexhaustive list of reasons to use this crate:
[42](https://docs.rs#42)
[43](https://docs.rs#43)* You want to analyze or use a [Thompson `NFA`](nfa::thompson::NFA) directly.
[44](https://docs.rs#44)* You want more powerful multi-pattern search than what is provided by
[45](https://docs.rs#45)`RegexSet` in the `regex` crate. All regex engines in this crate support
[46](https://docs.rs#46)multi-pattern searches.
[47](https://docs.rs#47)* You want to use one of the `regex` crate's internal engines directly because
[48](https://docs.rs#48)of some interesting configuration that isn't possible via the `regex` crate.
[49](https://docs.rs#49)For example, a [lazy DFA's configuration](hybrid::dfa::Config) exposes a
[50](https://docs.rs#50)dizzying number of options for controlling its execution.
[51](https://docs.rs#51)* You want to use the lower level search APIs. For example, both the [lazy
[52](https://docs.rs#52)DFA](hybrid::dfa) and [fully compiled DFAs](dfa) support searching by exploring
[53](https://docs.rs#53)the automaton one state at a time. This might be useful, for example, for
[54](https://docs.rs#54)stream searches or searches of strings stored in non-contiguous in memory.
[55](https://docs.rs#55)* You want to build a fully compiled DFA and then [use zero-copy
[56](https://docs.rs#56)deserialization](dfa::dense::DFA::from_bytes) to load it into memory and use
[57](https://docs.rs#57)it for searching. This use case is supported in core-only no-std/no-alloc
[58](https://docs.rs#58)environments.
[59](https://docs.rs#59)* You want to run [anchored searches](Input::anchored) without using the `^`
[60](https://docs.rs#60)anchor in your regex pattern.
[61](https://docs.rs#61)* You need to work-around contention issues with
[62](https://docs.rs#62)sharing a regex across multiple threads. The
[63](https://docs.rs#63)[`meta::Regex::search_with`](meta::Regex::search_with) API permits bypassing
[64](https://docs.rs#64)any kind of synchronization at all by requiring the caller to provide the
[65](https://docs.rs#65)mutable scratch spaced needed during a search.
[66](https://docs.rs#66)* You want to build your own regex engine on top of the `regex` crate's
[67](https://docs.rs#67)infrastructure.
[68](https://docs.rs#68)
[69](https://docs.rs#69)# Examples
[70](https://docs.rs#70)
[71](https://docs.rs#71)This section tries to identify a few interesting things you can do with this
[72](https://docs.rs#72)crate and demonstrates them.
[73](https://docs.rs#73)
[74](https://docs.rs#74)### Multi-pattern searches with capture groups
[75](https://docs.rs#75)
[76](https://docs.rs#76)One of the more frustrating limitations of `RegexSet` in the `regex` crate
[77](https://docs.rs#77)(at the time of writing) is that it doesn't report match positions. With this
[78](https://docs.rs#78)crate, multi-pattern support was intentionally designed in from the beginning,
[79](https://docs.rs#79)which means it works in all regex engines and even for capture groups as well.
[80](https://docs.rs#80)
[81](https://docs.rs#81)This example shows how to search for matches of multiple regexes, where each
[82](https://docs.rs#82)regex uses the same capture group names to parse different key-value formats.
[83](https://docs.rs#83)
[84](https://docs.rs#84)```
[85](https://docs.rs#85)use regex_automata::{meta::Regex, PatternID};
[86](https://docs.rs#86)
[87](https://docs.rs#87)let re = Regex::new_many(&[
[88](https://docs.rs#88)    r#"(?m)^(?<key>[[:word:]]+)=(?<val>[[:word:]]+)$"#,
[89](https://docs.rs#89)    r#"(?m)^(?<key>[[:word:]]+)="(?<val>[^"]+)"$"#,
[90](https://docs.rs#90)    r#"(?m)^(?<key>[[:word:]]+)='(?<val>[^']+)'$"#,
[91](https://docs.rs#91)    r#"(?m)^(?<key>[[:word:]]+):\s*(?<val>[[:word:]]+)$"#,
[92](https://docs.rs#92)])?;
[93](https://docs.rs#93)let hay = r#"
[94](https://docs.rs#94)best_album="Blow Your Face Out"
[95](https://docs.rs#95)best_quote='"then as it was, then again it will be"'
[96](https://docs.rs#96)best_year=1973
[97](https://docs.rs#97)best_simpsons_episode: HOMR
[98](https://docs.rs#98)"#;
[99](https://docs.rs#99)let mut kvs = vec![];
[100](https://docs.rs#100)for caps in re.captures_iter(hay) {
[101](https://docs.rs#101)    // N.B. One could use capture indices '1' and '2' here
[102](https://docs.rs#102)    // as well. Capture indices are local to each pattern.
[103](https://docs.rs#103)    // (Just like names are.)
[104](https://docs.rs#104)    let key = &hay[caps.get_group_by_name("key").unwrap()];
[105](https://docs.rs#105)    let val = &hay[caps.get_group_by_name("val").unwrap()];
[106](https://docs.rs#106)    kvs.push((key, val));
[107](https://docs.rs#107)}
[108](https://docs.rs#108)assert_eq!(kvs, vec![
[109](https://docs.rs#109)    ("best_album", "Blow Your Face Out"),
[110](https://docs.rs#110)    ("best_quote", "\"then as it was, then again it will be\""),
[111](https://docs.rs#111)    ("best_year", "1973"),
[112](https://docs.rs#112)    ("best_simpsons_episode", "HOMR"),
[113](https://docs.rs#113)]);
[114](https://docs.rs#114)
[115](https://docs.rs#115)# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
[116](https://docs.rs#116)```
[117](https://docs.rs#117)
[118](https://docs.rs#118)### Build a full DFA and walk it manually
[119](https://docs.rs#119)
[120](https://docs.rs#120)One of the regex engines in this crate is a fully compiled DFA. It takes worst
[121](https://docs.rs#121)case exponential time to build, but once built, it can be easily explored and
[122](https://docs.rs#122)used for searches. Here's a simple example that uses its lower level APIs to
[123](https://docs.rs#123)implement a simple anchored search by hand.
[124](https://docs.rs#124)
[125](https://docs.rs#125)```
[126](https://docs.rs#126)use regex_automata::{dfa::{Automaton, dense}, Input};
[127](https://docs.rs#127)
[128](https://docs.rs#128)let dfa = dense::DFA::new(r"(?-u)\b[A-Z]\w+z\b")?;
[129](https://docs.rs#129)let haystack = "Quartz";
[130](https://docs.rs#130)
[131](https://docs.rs#131)// The start state is determined by inspecting the position and the
[132](https://docs.rs#132)// initial bytes of the haystack.
[133](https://docs.rs#133)let mut state = dfa.start_state_forward(&Input::new(haystack))?;
[134](https://docs.rs#134)// Walk all the bytes in the haystack.
[135](https://docs.rs#135)for &b in haystack.as_bytes().iter() {
[136](https://docs.rs#136)    state = dfa.next_state(state, b);
[137](https://docs.rs#137)}
[138](https://docs.rs#138)// DFAs in this crate require an explicit
[139](https://docs.rs#139)// end-of-input transition if a search reaches
[140](https://docs.rs#140)// the end of a haystack.
[141](https://docs.rs#141)state = dfa.next_eoi_state(state);
[142](https://docs.rs#142)assert!(dfa.is_match_state(state));
[143](https://docs.rs#143)
[144](https://docs.rs#144)# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
[145](https://docs.rs#145)```
[146](https://docs.rs#146)
[147](https://docs.rs#147)Or do the same with a lazy DFA that avoids exponential worst case compile time,
[148](https://docs.rs#148)but requires mutable scratch space to lazily build the DFA during the search.
[149](https://docs.rs#149)
[150](https://docs.rs#150)```
[151](https://docs.rs#151)use regex_automata::{hybrid::dfa::DFA, Input};
[152](https://docs.rs#152)
[153](https://docs.rs#153)let dfa = DFA::new(r"(?-u)\b[A-Z]\w+z\b")?;
[154](https://docs.rs#154)let mut cache = dfa.create_cache();
[155](https://docs.rs#155)let hay = "Quartz";
[156](https://docs.rs#156)
[157](https://docs.rs#157)// The start state is determined by inspecting the position and the
[158](https://docs.rs#158)// initial bytes of the haystack.
[159](https://docs.rs#159)let mut state = dfa.start_state_forward(&mut cache, &Input::new(hay))?;
[160](https://docs.rs#160)// Walk all the bytes in the haystack.
[161](https://docs.rs#161)for &b in hay.as_bytes().iter() {
[162](https://docs.rs#162)    state = dfa.next_state(&mut cache, state, b)?;
[163](https://docs.rs#163)}
[164](https://docs.rs#164)// DFAs in this crate require an explicit
[165](https://docs.rs#165)// end-of-input transition if a search reaches
[166](https://docs.rs#166)// the end of a haystack.
[167](https://docs.rs#167)state = dfa.next_eoi_state(&mut cache, state)?;
[168](https://docs.rs#168)assert!(state.is_match());
[169](https://docs.rs#169)
[170](https://docs.rs#170)# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
[171](https://docs.rs#171)```
[172](https://docs.rs#172)
[173](https://docs.rs#173)### Find all overlapping matches
[174](https://docs.rs#174)
[175](https://docs.rs#175)This example shows how to build a DFA and use it to find all possible matches,
[176](https://docs.rs#176)including overlapping matches. A similar example will work with a lazy DFA as
[177](https://docs.rs#177)well. This also works with multiple patterns and will report all matches at the
[178](https://docs.rs#178)same position where multiple patterns match.
[179](https://docs.rs#179)
[180](https://docs.rs#180)```
[181](https://docs.rs#181)use regex_automata::{
[182](https://docs.rs#182)    dfa::{dense, Automaton, OverlappingState},
[183](https://docs.rs#183)    Input, MatchKind,
[184](https://docs.rs#184)};
[185](https://docs.rs#185)
[186](https://docs.rs#186)let dfa = dense::DFA::builder()
[187](https://docs.rs#187)    .configure(dense::DFA::config().match_kind(MatchKind::All))
[188](https://docs.rs#188)    .build(r"(?-u)\w{3,}")?;
[189](https://docs.rs#189)let input = Input::new("homer marge bart lisa maggie");
[190](https://docs.rs#190)let mut state = OverlappingState::start();
[191](https://docs.rs#191)
[192](https://docs.rs#192)let mut matches = vec![];
[193](https://docs.rs#193)while let Some(hm) = {
[194](https://docs.rs#194)    dfa.try_search_overlapping_fwd(&input, &mut state)?;
[195](https://docs.rs#195)    state.get_match()
[196](https://docs.rs#196)} {
[197](https://docs.rs#197)    matches.push(hm.offset());
[198](https://docs.rs#198)}
[199](https://docs.rs#199)assert_eq!(matches, vec![
[200](https://docs.rs#200)    3, 4, 5,        // hom, home, homer
[201](https://docs.rs#201)    9, 10, 11,      // mar, marg, marge
[202](https://docs.rs#202)    15, 16,         // bar, bart
[203](https://docs.rs#203)    20, 21,         // lis, lisa
[204](https://docs.rs#204)    25, 26, 27, 28, // mag, magg, maggi, maggie
[205](https://docs.rs#205)]);
[206](https://docs.rs#206)
[207](https://docs.rs#207)# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
[208](https://docs.rs#208)```
[209](https://docs.rs#209)
[210](https://docs.rs#210)# Available regex engines
[211](https://docs.rs#211)
[212](https://docs.rs#212)The following is a complete list of all regex engines provided by this crate,
[213](https://docs.rs#213)along with a very brief description of it and why you might want to use it.
[214](https://docs.rs#214)
[215](https://docs.rs#215)* [`dfa::regex::Regex`] is a regex engine that works on top of either
[216](https://docs.rs#216)[dense](dfa::dense) or [sparse](dfa::sparse) fully compiled DFAs. You might
[217](https://docs.rs#217)use a DFA if you need the fastest possible regex engine in this crate and can
[218](https://docs.rs#218)afford the exorbitant memory usage usually required by DFAs. Low level APIs on
[219](https://docs.rs#219)fully compiled DFAs are provided by the [`Automaton` trait](dfa::Automaton).
[220](https://docs.rs#220)Fully compiled dense DFAs can handle all regexes except for searching a regex
[221](https://docs.rs#221)with a Unicode word boundary on non-ASCII haystacks. A fully compiled DFA based
[222](https://docs.rs#222)regex can only report the start and end of each match.
[223](https://docs.rs#223)* [`hybrid::regex::Regex`] is a regex engine that works on top of a lazily
[224](https://docs.rs#224)built DFA. Its performance profile is very similar to that of fully compiled
[225](https://docs.rs#225)DFAs, but can be slower in some pathological cases. Fully compiled DFAs are
[226](https://docs.rs#226)also amenable to more optimizations, such as state acceleration, that aren't
[227](https://docs.rs#227)available in a lazy DFA. You might use this lazy DFA if you can't abide the
[228](https://docs.rs#228)worst case exponential compile time of a full DFA, but still want the DFA
[229](https://docs.rs#229)search performance in the vast majority of cases. A lazy DFA based regex can
[230](https://docs.rs#230)only report the start and end of each match.
[231](https://docs.rs#231)* [`dfa::onepass::DFA`] is a regex engine that is implemented as a DFA, but
[232](https://docs.rs#232)can report the matches of each capture group in addition to the start and end
[233](https://docs.rs#233)of each match. The catch is that it only works on a somewhat small subset of
[234](https://docs.rs#234)regexes known as "one-pass." You'll want to use this for cases when you need
[235](https://docs.rs#235)capture group matches and the regex is one-pass since it is likely to be faster
[236](https://docs.rs#236)than any alternative. A one-pass DFA can handle all types of regexes, but does
[237](https://docs.rs#237)have some reasonable limits on the number of capture groups it can handle.
[238](https://docs.rs#238)* [`nfa::thompson::backtrack::BoundedBacktracker`] is a regex engine that uses
[239](https://docs.rs#239)backtracking, but keeps track of the work it has done to avoid catastrophic
[240](https://docs.rs#240)backtracking. Like the one-pass DFA, it provides the matches of each capture
[241](https://docs.rs#241)group. It retains the `O(m * n)` worst case time bound. This tends to be slower
[242](https://docs.rs#242)than the one-pass DFA regex engine, but faster than the PikeVM. It can handle
[243](https://docs.rs#243)all types of regexes, but usually only works well with small haystacks and
[244](https://docs.rs#244)small regexes due to the memory required to avoid redoing work.
[245](https://docs.rs#245)* [`nfa::thompson::pikevm::PikeVM`] is a regex engine that can handle all
[246](https://docs.rs#246)regexes, of all sizes and provides capture group matches. It tends to be a tool
[247](https://docs.rs#247)of last resort because it is also usually the slowest regex engine.
[248](https://docs.rs#248)* [`meta::Regex`] is the meta regex engine that combines *all* of the above
[249](https://docs.rs#249)engines into one. The reason for this is that each of the engines above have
[250](https://docs.rs#250)their own caveats such as, "only handles a subset of regexes" or "is generally
[251](https://docs.rs#251)slow." The meta regex engine accounts for all of these caveats and composes
[252](https://docs.rs#252)the engines in a way that attempts to mitigate each engine's weaknesses while
[253](https://docs.rs#253)emphasizing its strengths. For example, it will attempt to run a lazy DFA even
[254](https://docs.rs#254)if it might fail. In which case, it will restart the search with a likely
[255](https://docs.rs#255)slower but more capable regex engine. The meta regex engine is what you should
[256](https://docs.rs#256)default to. Use one of the above engines directly only if you have a specific
[257](https://docs.rs#257)reason to.
[258](https://docs.rs#258)
[259](https://docs.rs#259)# API themes
[260](https://docs.rs#260)
[261](https://docs.rs#261)While each regex engine has its own APIs and configuration options, there are
[262](https://docs.rs#262)some general themes followed by all of them.
[263](https://docs.rs#263)
[264](https://docs.rs#264)### The `Input` abstraction
[265](https://docs.rs#265)
[266](https://docs.rs#266)Most search routines in this crate accept anything that implements
[267](https://docs.rs#267)`Into<Input>`. Both `&str` and `&[u8]` haystacks satisfy this constraint, which
[268](https://docs.rs#268)means that things like `engine.search("foo")` will work as you would expect.
[269](https://docs.rs#269)
[270](https://docs.rs#270)By virtue of accepting an `Into<Input>` though, callers can provide more than
[271](https://docs.rs#271)just a haystack. Indeed, the [`Input`] type has more details, but briefly,
[272](https://docs.rs#272)callers can use it to configure various aspects of the search:
[273](https://docs.rs#273)
[274](https://docs.rs#274)* The span of the haystack to search via [`Input::span`] or [`Input::range`],
[275](https://docs.rs#275)which might be a substring of the haystack.
[276](https://docs.rs#276)* Whether to run an anchored search or not via [`Input::anchored`]. This
[277](https://docs.rs#277)permits one to require matches to start at the same offset that the search
[278](https://docs.rs#278)started.
[279](https://docs.rs#279)* Whether to ask the regex engine to stop as soon as a match is seen via
[280](https://docs.rs#280)[`Input::earliest`]. This can be used to find the offset of a match as soon
[281](https://docs.rs#281)as it is known without waiting for the full leftmost-first match to be found.
[282](https://docs.rs#282)This can also be used to avoid the worst case `O(m * n^2)` time complexity
[283](https://docs.rs#283)of iteration.
[284](https://docs.rs#284)
[285](https://docs.rs#285)Some lower level search routines accept an `&Input` for performance reasons.
[286](https://docs.rs#286)In which case, `&Input::new("haystack")` can be used for a simple search.
[287](https://docs.rs#287)
[288](https://docs.rs#288)### Error reporting
[289](https://docs.rs#289)
[290](https://docs.rs#290)Most, but not all, regex engines in this crate can fail to execute a search.
[291](https://docs.rs#291)When a search fails, callers cannot determine whether or not a match exists.
[292](https://docs.rs#292)That is, the result is indeterminate.
[293](https://docs.rs#293)
[294](https://docs.rs#294)Search failure, in all cases in this crate, is represented by a [`MatchError`].
[295](https://docs.rs#295)Routines that can fail start with the `try_` prefix in their name. For example,
[296](https://docs.rs#296)[`hybrid::regex::Regex::try_search`] can fail for a number of reasons.
[297](https://docs.rs#297)Conversely, routines that either can't fail or can panic on failure lack the
[298](https://docs.rs#298)`try_` prefix. For example, [`hybrid::regex::Regex::find`] will panic in
[299](https://docs.rs#299)cases where [`hybrid::regex::Regex::try_search`] would return an error, and
[300](https://docs.rs#300)[`meta::Regex::find`] will never panic. Therefore, callers need to pay close
[301](https://docs.rs#301)attention to the panicking conditions in the documentation.
[302](https://docs.rs#302)
[303](https://docs.rs#303)In most cases, the reasons that a search fails are either predictable or
[304](https://docs.rs#304)configurable, albeit at some additional cost.
[305](https://docs.rs#305)
[306](https://docs.rs#306)An example of predictable failure is
[307](https://docs.rs#307)[`BoundedBacktracker::try_search`](nfa::thompson::backtrack::BoundedBacktracker::try_search).
[308](https://docs.rs#308)Namely, it fails whenever the multiplication of the haystack, the regex and some
[309](https://docs.rs#309)constant exceeds the
[310](https://docs.rs#310)[configured visited capacity](nfa::thompson::backtrack::Config::visited_capacity).
[311](https://docs.rs#311)Callers can predict the failure in terms of haystack length via the
[312](https://docs.rs#312)[`BoundedBacktracker::max_haystack_len`](nfa::thompson::backtrack::BoundedBacktracker::max_haystack_len)
[313](https://docs.rs#313)method. While this form of failure is technically avoidable by increasing the
[314](https://docs.rs#314)visited capacity, it isn't practical to do so for all inputs because the
[315](https://docs.rs#315)memory usage required for larger haystacks becomes impractically large. So in
[316](https://docs.rs#316)practice, if one is using the bounded backtracker, you really do have to deal
[317](https://docs.rs#317)with the failure.
[318](https://docs.rs#318)
[319](https://docs.rs#319)An example of configurable failure happens when one enables heuristic support
[320](https://docs.rs#320)for Unicode word boundaries in a DFA. Namely, since the DFAs in this crate
[321](https://docs.rs#321)(except for the one-pass DFA) do not support Unicode word boundaries on
[322](https://docs.rs#322)non-ASCII haystacks, building a DFA from an NFA that contains a Unicode word
[323](https://docs.rs#323)boundary will itself fail. However, one can configure DFAs to still be built in
[324](https://docs.rs#324)this case by
[325](https://docs.rs#325)[configuring heuristic support for Unicode word boundaries](hybrid::dfa::Config::unicode_word_boundary).
[326](https://docs.rs#326)If the NFA the DFA is built from contains a Unicode word boundary, then the
[327](https://docs.rs#327)DFA will still be built, but special transitions will be added to every state
[328](https://docs.rs#328)that cause the DFA to fail if any non-ASCII byte is seen. This failure happens
[329](https://docs.rs#329)at search time and it requires the caller to opt into this.
[330](https://docs.rs#330)
[331](https://docs.rs#331)There are other ways for regex engines to fail in this crate, but the above
[332](https://docs.rs#332)two should represent the general theme of failures one can find. Dealing
[333](https://docs.rs#333)with these failures is, in part, one the responsibilities of the [meta regex
[334](https://docs.rs#334)engine](meta). Notice, for example, that the meta regex engine exposes an API
[335](https://docs.rs#335)that never returns an error nor panics. It carefully manages all of the ways
[336](https://docs.rs#336)in which the regex engines can fail and either avoids the predictable ones
[337](https://docs.rs#337)entirely (e.g., the bounded backtracker) or reacts to configured failures by
[338](https://docs.rs#338)falling back to a different engine (e.g., the lazy DFA quitting because it saw
[339](https://docs.rs#339)a non-ASCII byte).
[340](https://docs.rs#340)
[341](https://docs.rs#341)### Configuration and Builders
[342](https://docs.rs#342)
[343](https://docs.rs#343)Most of the regex engines in this crate come with two types to facilitate
[344](https://docs.rs#344)building the regex engine: a `Config` and a `Builder`. A `Config` is usually
[345](https://docs.rs#345)specific to that particular regex engine, but other objects such as parsing and
[346](https://docs.rs#346)NFA compilation have `Config` types too. A `Builder` is the thing responsible
[347](https://docs.rs#347)for taking inputs (either pattern strings or already-parsed patterns or even
[348](https://docs.rs#348)NFAs directly) and turning them into an actual regex engine that can be used
[349](https://docs.rs#349)for searching.
[350](https://docs.rs#350)
[351](https://docs.rs#351)The main reason why building a regex engine is a bit complicated is because
[352](https://docs.rs#352)of the desire to permit composition with de-coupled components. For example,
[353](https://docs.rs#353)you might want to [manually construct a Thompson NFA](nfa::thompson::Builder)
[354](https://docs.rs#354)and then build a regex engine from it without ever using a regex parser
[355](https://docs.rs#355)at all. On the other hand, you might also want to build a regex engine directly
[356](https://docs.rs#356)from the concrete syntax. This demonstrates why regex engine construction is
[357](https://docs.rs#357)so flexible: it needs to support not just convenient construction, but also
[358](https://docs.rs#358)construction from parts built elsewhere.
[359](https://docs.rs#359)
[360](https://docs.rs#360)This is also in turn why there are many different `Config` structs in this
[361](https://docs.rs#361)crate. Let's look more closely at an example: [`hybrid::regex::Builder`]. It
[362](https://docs.rs#362)accepts three different `Config` types for configuring construction of a lazy
[363](https://docs.rs#363)DFA regex:
[364](https://docs.rs#364)
[365](https://docs.rs#365)* [`hybrid::regex::Builder::syntax`] accepts a
[366](https://docs.rs#366)[`util::syntax::Config`] for configuring the options found in the
[367](https://docs.rs#367)[`regex-syntax`](regex_syntax) crate. For example, whether to match
[368](https://docs.rs#368)case insensitively.
[369](https://docs.rs#369)* [`hybrid::regex::Builder::thompson`] accepts a [`nfa::thompson::Config`] for
[370](https://docs.rs#370)configuring construction of a [Thompson NFA](nfa::thompson::NFA). For example,
[371](https://docs.rs#371)whether to build an NFA that matches the reverse language described by the
[372](https://docs.rs#372)regex.
[373](https://docs.rs#373)* [`hybrid::regex::Builder::dfa`] accept a [`hybrid::dfa::Config`] for
[374](https://docs.rs#374)configuring construction of the pair of underlying lazy DFAs that make up the
[375](https://docs.rs#375)lazy DFA regex engine. For example, changing the capacity of the cache used to
[376](https://docs.rs#376)store the transition table.
[377](https://docs.rs#377)
[378](https://docs.rs#378)The lazy DFA regex engine uses all three of those configuration objects for
[379](https://docs.rs#379)methods like [`hybrid::regex::Builder::build`], which accepts a pattern
[380](https://docs.rs#380)string containing the concrete syntax of your regex. It uses the syntax
[381](https://docs.rs#381)configuration to parse it into an AST and translate it into an HIR. Then the
[382](https://docs.rs#382)NFA configuration when compiling the HIR into an NFA. And then finally the DFA
[383](https://docs.rs#383)configuration when lazily determinizing the NFA into a DFA.
[384](https://docs.rs#384)
[385](https://docs.rs#385)Notice though that the builder also has a
[386](https://docs.rs#386)[`hybrid::regex::Builder::build_from_dfas`] constructor. This permits callers
[387](https://docs.rs#387)to build the underlying pair of lazy DFAs themselves (one for the forward
[388](https://docs.rs#388)searching to find the end of a match and one for the reverse searching to find
[389](https://docs.rs#389)the start of a match), and then build the regex engine from them. The lazy
[390](https://docs.rs#390)DFAs, in turn, have their own builder that permits [construction directly from
[391](https://docs.rs#391)a Thompson NFA](hybrid::dfa::Builder::build_from_nfa). Continuing down the
[392](https://docs.rs#392)rabbit hole, a Thompson NFA has its own compiler that permits [construction
[393](https://docs.rs#393)directly from an HIR](nfa::thompson::Compiler::build_from_hir). The lazy DFA
[394](https://docs.rs#394)regex engine builder lets you follow this rabbit hole all the way down, but
[395](https://docs.rs#395)also provides convenience routines that do it for you when you don't need
[396](https://docs.rs#396)precise control over every component.
[397](https://docs.rs#397)
[398](https://docs.rs#398)The [meta regex engine](meta) is a good example of something that utilizes the
[399](https://docs.rs#399)full flexibility of these builders. It often needs not only precise control
[400](https://docs.rs#400)over each component, but also shares them across multiple regex engines.
[401](https://docs.rs#401)(Most sharing is done by internal reference accounting. For example, an
[402](https://docs.rs#402)[`NFA`](nfa::thompson::NFA) is reference counted internally which makes cloning
[403](https://docs.rs#403)cheap.)
[404](https://docs.rs#404)
[405](https://docs.rs#405)### Size limits
[406](https://docs.rs#406)
[407](https://docs.rs#407)Unlike the `regex` crate, the `regex-automata` crate specifically does not
[408](https://docs.rs#408)enable any size limits by default. That means users of this crate need to
[409](https://docs.rs#409)be quite careful when using untrusted patterns. Namely, because bounded
[410](https://docs.rs#410)repetitions can grow exponentially by stacking them, it is possible to build a
[411](https://docs.rs#411)very large internal regex object from just a small pattern string. For example,
[412](https://docs.rs#412)the NFA built from the pattern `a{10}{10}{10}{10}{10}{10}{10}` is over 240MB.
[413](https://docs.rs#413)
[414](https://docs.rs#414)There are multiple size limit options in this crate. If one or more size limits
[415](https://docs.rs#415)are relevant for the object you're building, they will be configurable via
[416](https://docs.rs#416)methods on a corresponding `Config` type.
[417](https://docs.rs#417)
[418](https://docs.rs#418)# Crate features
[419](https://docs.rs#419)
[420](https://docs.rs#420)This crate has a dizzying number of features. The main idea is to be able to
[421](https://docs.rs#421)control how much stuff you pull in for your specific use case, since the full
[422](https://docs.rs#422)crate is quite large and can dramatically increase compile times and binary
[423](https://docs.rs#423)size.
[424](https://docs.rs#424)
[425](https://docs.rs#425)The most barebones but useful configuration is to disable all default features
[426](https://docs.rs#426)and enable only `dfa-search`. This will bring in just the DFA deserialization
[427](https://docs.rs#427)and search routines without any dependency on `std` or `alloc`. This does
[428](https://docs.rs#428)require generating and serializing a DFA, and then storing it somewhere, but
[429](https://docs.rs#429)it permits regex searches in freestanding or embedded environments.
[430](https://docs.rs#430)
[431](https://docs.rs#431)Because there are so many features, they are split into a few groups.
[432](https://docs.rs#432)
[433](https://docs.rs#433)The default set of features is: `std`, `syntax`, `perf`, `unicode`, `meta`,
[434](https://docs.rs#434)`nfa`, `dfa` and `hybrid`. Basically, the default is to enable everything
[435](https://docs.rs#435)except for development related features like `logging`.
[436](https://docs.rs#436)
[437](https://docs.rs#437)### Ecosystem features
[438](https://docs.rs#438)
[439](https://docs.rs#439)* **std** - Enables use of the standard library. In terms of APIs, this usually
[440](https://docs.rs#440)just means that error types implement the `std::error::Error` trait. Otherwise,
[441](https://docs.rs#441)`std` sometimes enables the code to be faster, for example, using a `HashMap`
[442](https://docs.rs#442)instead of a `BTreeMap`. (The `std` feature matters more for dependencies like
[443](https://docs.rs#443)`aho-corasick` and `memchr`, where `std` is required to enable certain classes
[444](https://docs.rs#444)of SIMD optimizations.) Enabling `std` automatically enables `alloc`.
[445](https://docs.rs#445)* **alloc** - Enables use of the `alloc` library. This is required for most
[446](https://docs.rs#446)APIs in this crate. The main exception is deserializing and searching with
[447](https://docs.rs#447)fully compiled DFAs.
[448](https://docs.rs#448)* **logging** - Adds a dependency on the `log` crate and makes this crate emit
[449](https://docs.rs#449)log messages of varying degrees of utility. The log messages are especially
[450](https://docs.rs#450)useful in trying to understand what the meta regex engine is doing.
[451](https://docs.rs#451)
[452](https://docs.rs#452)### Performance features
[453](https://docs.rs#453)
[454](https://docs.rs#454)**Note**:
[455](https://docs.rs#455)  To get performance benefits offered by the SIMD, `std` must be enabled.
[456](https://docs.rs#456)  None of the `perf-*` features will enable `std` implicitly.
[457](https://docs.rs#457)
[458](https://docs.rs#458)* **perf** - Enables all of the below features.
[459](https://docs.rs#459)* **perf-inline** - When enabled, `inline(always)` is used in (many) strategic
[460](https://docs.rs#460)locations to help performance at the expense of longer compile times and
[461](https://docs.rs#461)increased binary size.
[462](https://docs.rs#462)* **perf-literal** - Enables all literal related optimizations.
[463](https://docs.rs#463)    * **perf-literal-substring** - Enables all single substring literal
[464](https://docs.rs#464)    optimizations. This includes adding a dependency on the `memchr` crate.
[465](https://docs.rs#465)    * **perf-literal-multisubstring** - Enables all multiple substring literal
[466](https://docs.rs#466)    optimizations. This includes adding a dependency on the `aho-corasick`
[467](https://docs.rs#467)    crate.
[468](https://docs.rs#468)
[469](https://docs.rs#469)### Unicode features
[470](https://docs.rs#470)
[471](https://docs.rs#471)* **unicode** -
[472](https://docs.rs#472)  Enables all Unicode features. This feature is enabled by default, and will
[473](https://docs.rs#473)  always cover all Unicode features, even if more are added in the future.
[474](https://docs.rs#474)* **unicode-age** -
[475](https://docs.rs#475)  Provide the data for the
[476](https://docs.rs#476)  [Unicode `Age` property](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr44/tr44-24.html#Character_Age).
[477](https://docs.rs#477)  This makes it possible to use classes like `\p{Age:6.0}` to refer to all
[478](https://docs.rs#478)  codepoints first introduced in Unicode 6.0
[479](https://docs.rs#479)* **unicode-bool** -
[480](https://docs.rs#480)  Provide the data for numerous Unicode boolean properties. The full list
[481](https://docs.rs#481)  is not included here, but contains properties like `Alphabetic`, `Emoji`,
[482](https://docs.rs#482)  `Lowercase`, `Math`, `Uppercase` and `White_Space`.
[483](https://docs.rs#483)* **unicode-case** -
[484](https://docs.rs#484)  Provide the data for case insensitive matching using
[485](https://docs.rs#485)  [Unicode's "simple loose matches" specification](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr18/#Simple_Loose_Matches).
[486](https://docs.rs#486)* **unicode-gencat** -
[487](https://docs.rs#487)  Provide the data for
[488](https://docs.rs#488)  [Unicode general categories](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr44/tr44-24.html#General_Category_Values).
[489](https://docs.rs#489)  This includes, but is not limited to, `Decimal_Number`, `Letter`,
[490](https://docs.rs#490)  `Math_Symbol`, `Number` and `Punctuation`.
[491](https://docs.rs#491)* **unicode-perl** -
[492](https://docs.rs#492)  Provide the data for supporting the Unicode-aware Perl character classes,
[493](https://docs.rs#493)  corresponding to `\w`, `\s` and `\d`. This is also necessary for using
[494](https://docs.rs#494)  Unicode-aware word boundary assertions. Note that if this feature is
[495](https://docs.rs#495)  disabled, the `\s` and `\d` character classes are still available if the
[496](https://docs.rs#496)  `unicode-bool` and `unicode-gencat` features are enabled, respectively.
[497](https://docs.rs#497)* **unicode-script** -
[498](https://docs.rs#498)  Provide the data for
[499](https://docs.rs#499)  [Unicode scripts and script extensions](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr24/).
[500](https://docs.rs#500)  This includes, but is not limited to, `Arabic`, `Cyrillic`, `Hebrew`,
[501](https://docs.rs#501)  `Latin` and `Thai`.
[502](https://docs.rs#502)* **unicode-segment** -
[503](https://docs.rs#503)  Provide the data necessary to provide the properties used to implement the
[504](https://docs.rs#504)  [Unicode text segmentation algorithms](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr29/).
[505](https://docs.rs#505)  This enables using classes like `\p{gcb=Extend}`, `\p{wb=Katakana}` and
[506](https://docs.rs#506)  `\p{sb=ATerm}`.
[507](https://docs.rs#507)* **unicode-word-boundary** -
[508](https://docs.rs#508)  Enables support for Unicode word boundaries, i.e., `\b`, in regexes. When
[509](https://docs.rs#509)  this and `unicode-perl` are enabled, then data tables from `regex-syntax` are
[510](https://docs.rs#510)  used to implement Unicode word boundaries. However, if `regex-syntax` isn't
[511](https://docs.rs#511)  enabled as a dependency then one can still enable this feature. It will
[512](https://docs.rs#512)  cause `regex-automata` to bundle its own data table that would otherwise be
[513](https://docs.rs#513)  redundant with `regex-syntax`'s table.
[514](https://docs.rs#514)
[515](https://docs.rs#515)### Regex engine features
[516](https://docs.rs#516)
[517](https://docs.rs#517)* **syntax** - Enables a dependency on `regex-syntax`. This makes APIs
[518](https://docs.rs#518)for building regex engines from pattern strings available. Without the
[519](https://docs.rs#519)`regex-syntax` dependency, the only way to build a regex engine is generally
[520](https://docs.rs#520)to deserialize a previously built DFA or to hand assemble an NFA using its
[521](https://docs.rs#521)[builder API](nfa::thompson::Builder). Once you have an NFA, you can build any
[522](https://docs.rs#522)of the regex engines in this crate. The `syntax` feature also enables `alloc`.
[523](https://docs.rs#523)* **meta** - Enables the meta regex engine. This also enables the `syntax` and
[524](https://docs.rs#524)`nfa-pikevm` features, as both are the minimal requirements needed. The meta
[525](https://docs.rs#525)regex engine benefits from enabling any of the other regex engines and will
[526](https://docs.rs#526)use them automatically when appropriate.
[527](https://docs.rs#527)* **nfa** - Enables all NFA related features below.
[528](https://docs.rs#528)    * **nfa-thompson** - Enables the Thompson NFA APIs. This enables `alloc`.
[529](https://docs.rs#529)    * **nfa-pikevm** - Enables the PikeVM regex engine. This enables
[530](https://docs.rs#530)    `nfa-thompson`.
[531](https://docs.rs#531)    * **nfa-backtrack** - Enables the bounded backtracker regex engine. This
[532](https://docs.rs#532)    enables `nfa-thompson`.
[533](https://docs.rs#533)* **dfa** - Enables all DFA related features below.
[534](https://docs.rs#534)    * **dfa-build** - Enables APIs for determinizing DFAs from NFAs. This
[535](https://docs.rs#535)    enables `nfa-thompson` and `dfa-search`.
[536](https://docs.rs#536)    * **dfa-search** - Enables APIs for searching with DFAs.
[537](https://docs.rs#537)    * **dfa-onepass** - Enables the one-pass DFA API. This enables
[538](https://docs.rs#538)    `nfa-thompson`.
[539](https://docs.rs#539)* **hybrid** - Enables the hybrid NFA/DFA or "lazy DFA" regex engine. This
[540](https://docs.rs#540)enables `alloc` and `nfa-thompson`.

# regex_automata::meta - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/regex-automata/0.4.14/regex_automata/meta/index.html

**crate feature**only.

`meta`## Expand description

Provides a regex matcher that composes several other regex matchers automatically.

This module is home to a meta [ Regex](https://docs.rs/struct.Regex.html), which provides a convenient high
level API for executing regular expressions in linear time.

[§](https://docs.rs#comparison-with-the-regex-crate)Comparison with the `regex` crate

A meta `Regex` is the implementation used directly by the `regex` crate.
Indeed, the `regex` crate API is essentially just a light wrapper over a meta
`Regex`. This means that if you need the full flexibility offered by this
API, then you should be able to switch to using this API directly without
any changes in match semantics or syntax. However, there are some API level
differences:

- The `regex`crate API returns match objects that include references to the haystack itself, which in turn makes it easy to access the matching strings without having to slice the haystack yourself. In contrast, a meta`Regex`returns match objects that only have offsets in them.
- At time of writing, a meta `Regex`doesn’t have some of the convenience routines that the`regex`crate has, such as replacements. Note though that`Captures::interpolate_string`
- A meta `Regex`supports the`Input``regex`crate. For example,`Input::anchored``^`.
- A meta `Regex`supports multi-pattern searching everywhere. Indeed, every`Match``PatternID``PatternID::ZERO``regex`crate has distinct`Regex`and a`RegexSet`APIs. The former only supports a single pattern, while the latter supports multiple patterns but cannot report the offsets of a match.
- A meta `Regex`provides the explicit capability of bypassing its internal memory pool for automatically acquiring mutable scratch space required by its internal regex engines. Namely, a`Cache``Regex::search_with`

# Regex in regex_automata::meta - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/regex-automata/0.4.14/regex_automata/meta/struct.Regex.html

`pub struct Regex { /* private fields */ }`**crate feature**only.

`meta`## Expand description

A regex matcher that works by composing several other regex matchers automatically.

In effect, a meta regex papers over a lot of the quirks or performance problems in each of the regex engines in this crate. Its goal is to provide an infallible and simple API that “just does the right thing” in the common case.

A meta regex is the implementation of a `Regex` in the `regex` crate.
Indeed, the `regex` crate API is essentially just a light wrapper over
this type. This includes the `regex` crate’s `RegexSet` API!

[§](https://docs.rs#composition)Composition

This is called a “meta” matcher precisely because it uses other regex matchers to provide a convenient high level regex API. Here are some examples of how other regex matchers are composed:

- When calling `Regex::captures``PikeVM`[lazy DFA](https://docs.rs/hybrid/index.html). Only when a match is found is a slower engine like`PikeVM`used to find the matching span for each capture group.
- While higher throughout engines like the lazy DFA cannot handle Unicode word boundaries in general, they can still be used on pure ASCII haystacks by pretending that Unicode word boundaries are just plain ASCII word boundaries. However, if a haystack is not ASCII, the meta regex engine will automatically switch to a (possibly slower) regex engine that supports Unicode word boundaries in general.
- In some cases where a regex pattern is just a simple literal or a small set of literals, an actual regex engine won’t be used at all. Instead, substring or multi-substring search algorithms will be employed.

There are many other forms of composition happening too, but the above
should give a general idea. In particular, it may perhaps be surprising
that *multiple* regex engines might get executed for a single search. That
is, the decision of what regex engine to use is not *just* based on the
pattern, but also based on the dynamic execution of the search itself.

The primary reason for this composition is performance. The fundamental tension is that the faster engines tend to be less capable, and the more capable engines tend to be slower.

Note that the forms of composition that are allowed are determined by
compile time crate features and configuration. For example, if the `hybrid`
feature isn’t enabled, or if [ Config::hybrid](https://docs.rs/struct.Config.html#method.hybrid) has been disabled, then the
meta regex engine will never use a lazy DFA.

[§](https://docs.rs#synchronization-and-cloning)Synchronization and cloning

Most of the regex engines in this crate require some kind of mutable
“scratch” space to read and write from while performing a search. Since
a meta regex composes these regex engines, a meta regex also requires
mutable scratch space. This scratch space is called a [ Cache](https://docs.rs/struct.Cache.html).

Most regex engines *also* usually have a read-only component, typically
a [Thompson  NFA](https://docs.rs/nfa/thompson/struct.NFA.html).

In order to make the `Regex` API convenient, most of the routines hide
the fact that a `Cache` is needed at all. To achieve this, a [memory
pool](https://docs.rs/util/pool/struct.Pool.html) is used internally to retrieve `Cache`
values in a thread safe way that also permits reuse. This in turn implies
that every such search call requires some form of synchronization. Usually
this synchronization is fast enough to not notice, but in some cases, it
can be a bottleneck. This typically occurs when all of the following are
true:

- The same `Regex`is shared across multiple threads simultaneously, usually via a`util::lazy::Lazy``once_cell`or`lazy_static`crates.
- The primary unit of work in each thread is a regex search.
- Searches are run on very short haystacks.

This particular case can lead to high contention on the pool used by a
`Regex` internally, which can in turn increase latency to a noticeable
effect. This cost can be mitigated in one of the following ways:

- Use a distinct copy of a `Regex`in each thread, usually by cloning it. Cloning a`Regex`*does not*do a deep copy of its read-only component. But it does lead to each`Regex`having its own memory pool, which in turn eliminates the problem of contention. In general, this technique should not result in any additional memory usage when compared to sharing the same`Regex`across multiple threads simultaneously.
- Use lower level APIs, like `Regex::search_with``Cache`explicitly. In this case, it is up to you to determine how best to provide a`Cache`. For example, you might put a`Cache`in thread-local storage if your use case allows for it.

Overall, this is an issue that happens rarely in practice, but it can happen.

[§](https://docs.rs#warning-spin-locks-may-be-used-in-alloc-only-mode)Warning: spin-locks may be used in alloc-only mode

When this crate is built without the `std` feature and the high level APIs
on a `Regex` are used, then a spin-lock will be used to synchronize access
to an internal pool of `Cache` values. This may be undesirable because
a spin-lock is [effectively impossible to implement correctly in user
space](https://matklad.github.io/2020/01/02/spinlocks-considered-harmful.html). That is, more concretely, the spin-lock could
result in a deadlock.

If one wants to avoid the use of spin-locks when the `std` feature is
disabled, then you must use APIs that accept a `Cache` value explicitly.
For example, [ Regex::search_with](https://docs.rs/struct.Regex.html#method.search_with).

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use regex_automata::meta::Regex;
let re = Regex::new(r"^[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}$")?;
assert!(re.is_match("2010-03-14"));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-anchored-search)Example: anchored search

This example shows how to use [ Input::anchored](https://docs.rs/struct.Input.html#method.anchored) to run an anchored
search, even when the regex pattern itself isn’t anchored. An anchored
search guarantees that if a match is found, then the start offset of the
match corresponds to the offset at which the search was started.

```
use regex_automata::{meta::Regex, Anchored, Input, Match};
let re = Regex::new(r"\bfoo\b")?;
let input = Input::new("xx foo xx").range(3..).anchored(Anchored::Yes);
// The offsets are in terms of the original haystack.
assert_eq!(Some(Match::must(0, 3..6)), re.find(input));
// Notice that no match occurs here, because \b still takes the
// surrounding context into account, even if it means looking back
// before the start of your search.
let hay = "xxfoo xx";
let input = Input::new(hay).range(2..).anchored(Anchored::Yes);
assert_eq!(None, re.find(input));
// Indeed, you cannot achieve the above by simply slicing the
// haystack itself, since the regex engine can't see the
// surrounding context. This is why 'Input' permits setting
// the bounds of a search!
let input = Input::new(&hay[2..]).anchored(Anchored::Yes);
// WRONG!
assert_eq!(Some(Match::must(0, 0..3)), re.find(input));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-earliest-search)Example: earliest search

This example shows how to use [ Input::earliest](https://docs.rs/struct.Input.html#method.earliest) to run a search that
might stop before finding the typical leftmost match.

```
use regex_automata::{meta::Regex, Anchored, Input, Match};
let re = Regex::new(r"[a-z]{3}|b")?;
let input = Input::new("abc").earliest(true);
assert_eq!(Some(Match::must(0, 1..2)), re.find(input));
// Note that "earliest" isn't really a match semantic unto itself.
// Instead, it is merely an instruction to whatever regex engine
// gets used internally to quit as soon as it can. For example,
// this regex uses a different search technique, and winds up
// producing a different (but valid) match!
let re = Regex::new(r"abc|b")?;
let input = Input::new("abc").earliest(true);
assert_eq!(Some(Match::must(0, 0..3)), re.find(input));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-change-the-line-terminator)Example: change the line terminator

This example shows how to enable multi-line mode by default and change the line terminator to the NUL byte:

```
use regex_automata::{meta::Regex, util::syntax, Match};
let re = Regex::builder()
    .syntax(syntax::Config::new().multi_line(true))
    .configure(Regex::config().line_terminator(b'\x00'))
    .build(r"^foo$")?;
let hay = "\x00foo\x00";
assert_eq!(Some(Match::must(0, 1..4)), re.find(hay));
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Builds a `Regex` from a single pattern string using the default

If there was a problem parsing the pattern or a problem turning it into a regex matcher, then an error is returned.

with a

`Config`[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

```
use regex_automata::{meta::Regex, Match};
let re = Regex::new(r"(?Rm)^foo$")?;
let hay = "\r\nfoo\r\n";
assert_eq!(Some(Match::must(0, 2..5)), re.find(hay));
```
Builds a `Regex` from many pattern strings using the default
configuration.

If there was a problem parsing any of the patterns or a problem turning them into a regex matcher, then an error is returned.

If you want to change the configuration of a `Regex`, use a [ Builder](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html)
with a

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Config.html)

`Config`[§](https://docs.rs#example-simple-lexer)Example: simple lexer

This simplistic example leverages the multi-pattern support to build a simple little lexer. The pattern ID in the match tells you which regex matched, which in turn might be used to map back to the “type” of the token returned by the lexer.

```
use regex_automata::{meta::Regex, Match};
let re = Regex::new_many(&[
    r"[[:space:]]",
    r"[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9_]+",
    r"->",
    r".",
])?;
let haystack = "fn is_boss(bruce: i32, springsteen: String) -> bool;";
let matches: Vec<Match> = re.find_iter(haystack).collect();
assert_eq!(matches, vec![
    Match::must(1, 0..2),   // 'fn'
    Match::must(0, 2..3),   // ' '
    Match::must(1, 3..10),  // 'is_boss'
    Match::must(3, 10..11), // '('
    Match::must(1, 11..16), // 'bruce'
    Match::must(3, 16..17), // ':'
    Match::must(0, 17..18), // ' '
    Match::must(1, 18..21), // 'i32'
    Match::must(3, 21..22), // ','
    Match::must(0, 22..23), // ' '
    Match::must(1, 23..34), // 'springsteen'
    Match::must(3, 34..35), // ':'
    Match::must(0, 35..36), // ' '
    Match::must(1, 36..42), // 'String'
    Match::must(3, 42..43), // ')'
    Match::must(0, 43..44), // ' '
    Match::must(2, 44..46), // '->'
    Match::must(0, 46..47), // ' '
    Match::must(1, 47..51), // 'bool'
    Match::must(3, 51..52), // ';'
]);
```
One can write a lexer like the above using a regex like
`(?P<space>[[:space:]])|(?P<ident>[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9_]+)|...`,
but then you need to ask whether capture group matched to determine
which branch in the regex matched, and thus, which token the match
corresponds to. In contrast, the above example includes the pattern ID
in the match. There’s no need to use capture groups at all.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-finding-the-pattern-that-caused-an-error)Example: finding the pattern that caused an error

When a syntax error occurs, it is possible to ask which pattern caused the syntax error.

```
use regex_automata::{meta::Regex, PatternID};
let err = Regex::new_many(&["a", "b", r"\p{Foo}", "c"]).unwrap_err();
assert_eq!(Some(PatternID::must(2)), err.pattern());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-zero-patterns-is-valid)Example: zero patterns is valid

Building a regex with zero patterns results in a regex that never matches anything. Because this routine is generic, passing an empty slice usually requires a turbo-fish (or something else to help type inference).

```
use regex_automata::{meta::Regex, util::syntax, Match};
let re = Regex::new_many::<&str>(&[])?;
assert_eq!(None, re.find(""));
```
Return a default configuration for a `Regex`.

This is a convenience routine to avoid needing to import the [ Config](https://docs.rs/struct.Config.html)
type when customizing the construction of a

`Regex`.[§](https://docs.rs#example-lower-the-nfa-size-limit)Example: lower the NFA size limit

In some cases, the default size limit might be too big. The size limit can be lowered, which will prevent large regex patterns from compiling.

```
use regex_automata::meta::Regex;
let result = Regex::builder()
    .configure(Regex::config().nfa_size_limit(Some(20 * (1<<10))))
    // Not even 20KB is enough to build a single large Unicode class!
    .build(r"\pL");
assert!(result.is_err());
```
Return a builder for configuring the construction of a `Regex`.

This is a convenience routine to avoid needing to import the
[ Builder](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html) type in common cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-change-the-line-terminator-1)Example: change the line terminator

This example shows how to enable multi-line mode by default and change the line terminator to the NUL byte:

```
use regex_automata::{meta::Regex, util::syntax, Match};
let re = Regex::builder()
    .syntax(syntax::Config::new().multi_line(true))
    .configure(Regex::config().line_terminator(b'\x00'))
    .build(r"^foo$")?;
let hay = "\x00foo\x00";
assert_eq!(Some(Match::must(0, 1..4)), re.find(hay));
```
Returns true if and only if this regex matches the given haystack.

This routine may short circuit if it knows that scanning future input
will never lead to a different result. (Consider how this might make
a difference given the regex `a+` on the haystack `aaaaaaaaaaaaaaa`.
This routine *may* stop after it sees the first `a`, but routines like
`find` need to continue searching because `+` is greedy by default.)

[§](https://docs.rs#example-2)Example

```
use regex_automata::meta::Regex;
let re = Regex::new("foo[0-9]+bar")?;
assert!(re.is_match("foo12345bar"));
assert!(!re.is_match("foobar"));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-consistency-with-search-apis)Example: consistency with search APIs

`is_match` is guaranteed to return `true` whenever `find` returns a
match. This includes searches that are executed entirely within a
codepoint:

```
use regex_automata::{meta::Regex, Input};
let re = Regex::new("a*")?;
// This doesn't match because the default configuration bans empty
// matches from splitting a codepoint.
assert!(!re.is_match(Input::new("☃").span(1..2)));
assert_eq!(None, re.find(Input::new("☃").span(1..2)));
```
Notice that when UTF-8 mode is disabled, then the above reports a match because the restriction against zero-width matches that split a codepoint has been lifted:

```
use regex_automata::{meta::Regex, Input, Match};
let re = Regex::builder()
    .configure(Regex::config().utf8_empty(false))
    .build("a*")?;
assert!(re.is_match(Input::new("☃").span(1..2)));
assert_eq!(
    Some(Match::must(0, 1..1)),
    re.find(Input::new("☃").span(1..2)),
);
```
A similar idea applies when using line anchors with CRLF mode enabled,
which prevents them from matching between a `\r` and a `\n`.

```
use regex_automata::{meta::Regex, Input, Match};
let re = Regex::new(r"(?Rm:$)")?;
assert!(!re.is_match(Input::new("\r\n").span(1..1)));
// A regular line anchor, which only considers \n as a
// line terminator, will match.
let re = Regex::new(r"(?m:$)")?;
assert!(re.is_match(Input::new("\r\n").span(1..1)));
```
Executes a leftmost search and returns the first match that is found, if one exists.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-3)Example

```
use regex_automata::{meta::Regex, Match};
let re = Regex::new("foo[0-9]+")?;
assert_eq!(Some(Match::must(0, 0..8)), re.find("foo12345"));
```
Executes a leftmost forward search and writes the spans of capturing
groups that participated in a match into the provided [ Captures](https://docs.rs/util/captures/struct.Captures.html)
value. If no match was found, then

[is guaranteed to return](https://docs.rs/util/captures/struct.Captures.html#method.is_match)

`Captures::is_match``false`.[§](https://docs.rs#example-4)Example

```
use regex_automata::{meta::Regex, Span};
let re = Regex::new(r"^([0-9]{4})-([0-9]{2})-([0-9]{2})$")?;
let mut caps = re.create_captures();
re.captures("2010-03-14", &mut caps);
assert!(caps.is_match());
assert_eq!(Some(Span::from(0..4)), caps.get_group(1));
assert_eq!(Some(Span::from(5..7)), caps.get_group(2));
assert_eq!(Some(Span::from(8..10)), caps.get_group(3));
```
Returns an iterator over all non-overlapping leftmost matches in the given haystack. If no match exists, then the iterator yields no elements.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-5)Example

```
use regex_automata::{meta::Regex, Match};
let re = Regex::new("foo[0-9]+")?;
let haystack = "foo1 foo12 foo123";
let matches: Vec<Match> = re.find_iter(haystack).collect();
assert_eq!(matches, vec![
    Match::must(0, 0..4),
    Match::must(0, 5..10),
    Match::must(0, 11..17),
]);
```

#### pub fn [captures_iter](https://docs.rs#method.captures_iter)<'r, 'h, I: [Into](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html)<[Input](https://docs.rs/struct.Input.html)<'h>>>(
